title: She Outranked Kohli and Rohit on a List Headlined by LeBron. Smriti Mandhana Is the Only Indian on TIME's 100 Most Influential in Sports.
excerpt: The India vice-captain is the lone Indian athlete — and one of just two cricketers — on TIME's 2026 list, placed in the 'Titans' tier alongside Messi, Ronaldo and Alcaraz.
body:
India's women's cricket vice-captain Smriti Mandhana has been named to TIME magazine's list of the 100 Most Influential People in Sports for 2026 — the only Indian athlete on a roster headlined by LeBron James and crowded with names like Lionel Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo, Carlos Alcaraz, Eileen Gu and Victor Wembanyama. For a country that defines itself through cricket, the detail that lands hardest is this: the lone Indian on the most exclusive sports list of the year is a 29-year-old left-handed opener from Sangli, not a star of the men's game.

## A Titan, Ahead of Kohli and Rohit

TIME placed Mandhana in its "Titans" category, the tier reserved for the established giants of world sport. She is one of only two cricketers on the entire list, sharing that distinction with South Africa's Test captain Temba Bavuma. Conspicuously, the two biggest names in Indian men's cricket — Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma — do not appear at all. For a generation of fans raised to believe influence in Indian sport flows through the men's dressing room, the omission is its own quiet statement.

Charlie Campbell, TIME's editor-at-large, summed up the case for her inclusion in a single phrase: "The records keep tumbling in for Smriti Mandhana."

## The Records Behind the Recognition

The numbers are staggering. Mandhana was the first Indian woman to score a double century in a domestic one-day game, and the first Indian woman — man or woman, in fact, only she has done it for India's women — to score a century in all three international formats. She is a joint holder, alongside Australia's Meg Lanning, of the record for most centuries in women's international cricket, with 17. In 2025 she became the first woman ever to pass 1,000 ODI runs in a single calendar year, finishing with 1,362, after she had already set the record for most international runs across formats by a woman in 2024 and then broken her own mark a year later.

Across 167 women's T20 internationals she has piled up 4,401 runs, making her India's highest run-scorer in the format. Those performances earned her the BBC Indian Sportswoman of the Year award for 2025.

## Team Honours She Values Most

TIME was careful to note that Mandhana is "proudest of the team honors she is also accumulating." She captained Royal Challengers Bengaluru to Women's Premier League titles in both 2024 and 2026, turning a franchise that had struggled in the league's early seasons into repeat champions. And she was vice-captain when India lifted the ICC Women's World Cup last year, finishing as one of the tournament's top run-scorers in a campaign that finally delivered the global trophy that had eluded Indian women's cricket for decades.

The recognition arrives mid-tournament. Mandhana is in England right now, leading India's batting at the ICC Women's T20 World Cup, where the team opened with a commanding 64-run win over Pakistan and Mandhana herself made a brisk 68 off 44 balls at Edgbaston after being dropped twice.

## Why the Diaspora Should Care

For Indian families in the United States, Britain and Canada, Mandhana's place on a list dominated by Western sporting royalty is a marker of arrival. The diaspora has long watched its cultural touchstones — Bollywood, cricket, food — gain global currency. But seeing an Indian woman cricketer ranked among the most influential figures in world sport, ahead of household names from the men's game, reframes what representation looks like for daughters growing up far from home.

Women's cricket is also the fastest-growing arm of the sport in diaspora hubs. The Women's Premier League is now broadcast across North America and the UK, the WPL's 2026 final drew record overseas viewership, and youth leagues from New Jersey to Surrey are seeing more girls of Indian origin pick up a bat. Mandhana, with RCB's two titles and a global magazine cover's worth of recognition, has become the face many of them point to.

## What's Next

The immediate stage is the T20 World Cup, where India will fancy their chances of a deep run after the World Cup triumph of last year. Beyond that, Mandhana's trajectory points toward the 2027 calendar and a leadership role that grows with every series. The TIME honour is not a career retrospective; at 29, she is still adding records. As Campbell put it, they keep tumbling in — and the world is finally counting.
